summary: Montenegro lets citizens of the EU, UK, US and around 100 other countries visit visa-free for up to 90 days (30 days for Russia, Belarus and a few others), and travelers who do need a visa can instead enter for up to 30 days on a valid Schengen, US, UK or Irish visa or residence permit.

passportValidity.text: Your passport should be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from Montenegro — some sources cite 3 months from arrival; keep a comfortable margin and confirm with the embassy if in doubt.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Montenegro

travelInsurance.text: Not a condition of entry for visa-free visitors, though visa applicants must show travel health insurance for the stay. EU EHIC cards are not valid in Montenegro, so private cover is strongly recommended.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Montenegro

onwardTicket.text: Not routinely checked, but border officers may ask about return plans, accommodation and the purpose of your visit.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Montenegro

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published for tourists; border officers may ask visitors to show sufficient means for their stay.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Montenegro

declarations.name: Tourist registration (white card)
declarations.text: All foreign visitors must be registered with the local tourist organization or police within 24 hours of arrival. Hotels do this automatically; if you stay in a private apartment your host (or you) must register and pay the small nightly tourist tax. Keep the registration slip. It can be asked for on departure.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Montenegro

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be declared on entry and exit.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Montenegro

payments.text: Cards work in hotels, supermarkets and most coastal restaurants, but keep euro cash for taxis, market stalls, small konobas and anywhere inland.

safety.text: Montenegro is generally safe for visitors, with low violent crime against tourists. Watch for pickpocketing and car break-ins at busy coastal resorts in summer, and take care on narrow mountain roads.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Montenegro travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September is beach season on the Adriatic; June and September give warm sea without the July–August crush, and late spring is ideal for Durmitor and the mountains.

idp.text: Montenegro is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Montenegro is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Montenegro yet.

tips.text: Your accommodation must register you with the local tourist board within 24 hours — hotels do it automatically, but private hosts sometimes forget; ask for the registration slip and keep it until you leave.
Montenegro uses the euro even though it is not an EU member. No currency exchange needed if you arrive from the eurozone, but bring cash for small places.
The Bay of Kotor and Budva are extremely crowded in July and August, with cruise-ship surges in Kotor's old town — June and September offer the same swimming with far fewer people.
If your nationality needs a visa but you hold a valid Schengen, US, UK or Irish visa or residence permit, you can enter Montenegro visa-free for up to 30 days.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Montenegro?
faq.answer: Most visitors don't: citizens of the EU, UK, US, Canada, Australia, Japan and around 100 other countries can stay up to 90 days visa-free, while Russians, Belarusians and Kazakhs get 30 days. Nationalities that do need a visa can either apply at a Montenegrin embassy or enter on a valid Schengen, US, UK or Irish visa or residence permit for up to 30 days.

faq.question: Can I enter Montenegro with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes — holders of a valid Schengen visa or a Schengen-country residence permit (and equally US, UK or Irish visas and permits) may enter and stay up to 30 days without a Montenegrin visa, as long as the document remains valid. Confirm current terms with an embassy before travel.

faq.question: How long can US citizens stay in Montenegro?
faq.answer: US passport holders can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period without a visa. Montenegro is not in the Schengen Area, so this allowance is separate from your Schengen 90/180 days.

faq.question: Does Montenegro use the euro?
faq.answer: Yes — Montenegro adopted the euro unilaterally and it is the only legal tender, even though the country is not an EU member. Cards are widely accepted on the coast, but carry some cash.

faq.question: Do Russian citizens need a visa for Montenegro?
faq.answer: No — Russian citizens can currently enter visa-free for up to 30 days. In past summer seasons the allowance was temporarily extended, and terms can change, so confirm the current rules before traveling.

faq.question: Can EU citizens enter Montenegro with just an ID card?
faq.answer: Yes — EU citizens (and neighboring Western Balkan citizens) can enter with a national ID card for short stays of up to 30 days. For a full 90-day stay, or to be safe at all crossings, carry a passport.
